records.source: Μετὰ ταῦτα ἐφανέρωσεν ἑαυτὸν πάλιν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Τιβεριάδος· ἐφανέρωσεν δὲ οὕτως.
records.gloss: After these things revealed himself again the Jesus to the disciples at the sea of the Tiberias; he revealed now thus.

L.1: After these things Jesus revealed {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias; and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} revealed [{{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}] in this way.

R.1: Later, Jesus showed {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} to the disciples again. It was beside the Sea of Tiberias, which is another name for the Sea of Galilee. This is how it happened.

decisions.choice: revealed himself: made himself known, showed himself openly
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring into the open what was hidden. John used it of the glory Jesus revealed at Cana (2:11) and of his being revealed to Israel (1:31). Here the risen Jesus shows himself to his disciples when and as he chooses; at first they do not know him (verse 4). The same verb opens this story and closes it (verse 14).

decisions.choice: the Sea of Tiberias: the lake of Galilee
decisions.reason: John gave both names for the lake at 6:1; here he uses only the newer one, taken from the city of Tiberias that Herod Antipas built on its western shore. The scene has moved from Jerusalem back to Galilee, where several of the disciples came from and where some of them had been fishermen (Mark 1:16-20).

decisions.choice: After these things: a loose link back to the appearances of chapter 20
decisions.reason: John often moves to a new episode with this phrase and gives no length of time (5:1; 6:1; 7:1). The words of 20:30-31 read like the close of the book, since they state why it was written; chapter 21 follows them with one more appearance and a second closing (21:24-25), so it may be read as an epilogue to the Gospel. No known manuscript of John ends at 20:31.

decisions.choice: revealed (L, B); showed (R); It happened in this way (B); This is how it happened (R)
decisions.reason: As at 2:11, Literal and Balanced say "revealed" and Readable the plainer "showed". The short second clause introduces the story that follows, so Balanced and Readable turn it into a sentence of its own.

decisions.choice: which is another name for the Sea of Galilee
decisions.reason: Readable tells the reader that this is the lake of chapter 6 under its other name (meaning decision m2), as Readable did at 6:1.

records.heading: Jesus appears by the sea

records.source: ἦσαν ὁμοῦ Σίμων Πέτρος καὶ Θωμᾶς ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος καὶ Ναθαναὴλ ὁ ἀπὸ Κανὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας καὶ οἱ τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου καὶ ἄλλοι ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ δύο.
records.gloss: Were together Simon Peter and Thomas the [one] being called Didymus and Nathanael the [one] from Cana of the Galilee and the [ones] of the Zebedee and others of the disciples of him two.

L.2: There were together Simon Peter, and Thomas, the [one] called Didymus, and Nathanael, the [one] from Cana of Galilee, and the [sons] of Zebedee, and two others of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples.

R.2: Some of the disciples were together. Simon Peter was there, and Thomas, who was called the Twin. Nathanael was there too. He came from the town of Cana in Galilee. The sons of Zebedee were there, and two other disciples of Jesus.

decisions.choice: Thomas called Didymus: both names mean "twin"
decisions.reason: As at 11:16 and 20:24, John gives the Greek word for Thomas's Semitic name. Thomas is the disciple who confessed "My Lord and my God" a week after the resurrection (20:28).

decisions.choice: Nathanael from Cana: the disciple Jesus met in 1:45-51
decisions.reason: Nathanael appears only here and in 1:45-51, where Jesus saw him under the fig tree and Nathanael called him the Son of God and the King of Israel. Only here does John say that he came from Cana, the village where Jesus did his first sign (2:1, 11) and healed the official's son from afar (4:46-54).

decisions.choice: the ones of Zebedee: the sons of Zebedee, James and John
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "the ones of Zebedee", the usual way of naming a man's sons. The other Gospels name them as James and John, fishermen on this lake (Mark 1:19-20; Matthew 4:21). This is the only time John mentions them, and he never gives their names.

decisions.choice: two others of his disciples: two more disciples, not named
decisions.reason: With these two the group comes to seven. John does not say who the two were or whether they were among the Twelve. The disciple whom Jesus loved (verse 7) must be one of the seven, but John does not say which.

decisions.choice: [sons] of Zebedee (L); Zebedee's sons (B); The sons of Zebedee (R)
decisions.reason: English needs a noun where the Greek has only the article (meaning decision m3); Literal brackets it.

decisions.choice: called Didymus, which means Twin (B); called the Twin (R); the town of Cana (R); disciples of Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: As at 11:16 and 20:24, Balanced adds what the name means and Readable gives only the meaning. Readable says that Cana was a town, breaks the list into short sentences and names Jesus for "his".

records.source: λέγει αὐτοῖς Σίμων Πέτρος· Ὑπάγω ἁλιεύειν· λέγουσιν αὐτῷ· Ἐρχόμεθα καὶ ἡμεῖς σὺν σοί.
records.gloss: Says to them Simon Peter: I am going away to fish; they say to him: Are coming also we with you.

L.3: Simon Peter says to them, "I am going off to fish." They say to him, "We also are coming with you."

R.3: Simon Peter told the others, "I am going out to fish." They said, "We will come with you."

decisions.choice: I am going to fish: Peter goes back to the lake, and John does not say why
alternatives: Peter gives up his calling and returns to his old trade
a night's work to earn food
decisions.reason: The other Gospels tell that Peter and Andrew were fishermen on this lake when Jesus called them (Mark 1:16-18; Luke 5:1-11), and that the disciples were told to go to Galilee to meet the risen Jesus (Matthew 28:7, 10; Mark 16:7). John gives no reason for the fishing trip and makes no judgment on it. The story that follows turns on what they catch without Jesus and what they catch at his word.

decisions.choice: We also are coming: the other six go with Peter at once
decisions.reason: The present tense states a decision being carried out now. "They" are the other disciples named in verse 2; Peter leads and they follow.

decisions.choice: historic present at Literal ("says", "see", "comes", "takes", "gives"); past tense at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John, Literal keeps the present tense with which John tells some past events ("says" in 21:3, 5, 7, 10, 12; "see" in 21:9; "comes", "takes" and "gives" in 21:13), which makes the story vivid. Balanced and Readable use the past, as English tells a story. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: going out fishing (B); going out to fish (R); We will come with you (B, R); told the others (R)
alternatives: I am going off to fish; We also are coming with you (Literal)
decisions.reason: English uses "will" for a decision made on the spot, where Greek can use the present (meaning decision m2). Readable says who "them" are.

records.source: ἐξῆλθον καὶ ἐνέβησαν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, καὶ ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ νυκτὶ ἐπίασαν οὐδέν.
records.gloss: They went out and got into the boat, and in that the night they caught nothing.

L.3: They went out and got into the boat, and during that night they caught nothing.

R.3: So they went off and climbed into the boat. But that whole night they did not catch anything.

decisions.choice: that night: fishing with nets was done at night
decisions.reason: Fishermen on the lake worked through the night, when the fish come nearer the surface and do not see the nets, and brought in their catch at dawn (Luke 5:5, "we worked hard all night").

decisions.choice: they caught nothing: a whole night's work without result, before a great catch at Jesus's word
alternatives: no echo of the earlier story
decisions.reason: Luke tells of another night when Peter caught nothing, and of a great catch when he let down the nets at Jesus's word (Luke 5:4-7). John does not mention that story, but readers who knew it may hear it again here, after the resurrection. Jesus had said, "apart from me you can do nothing" (15:5).

decisions.choice: but all that night (B); But that whole night (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek joins the clauses with "and", but the sense is a contrast: they went out to fish and caught nothing. "All" or "whole" says what "that night" implies, that they fished the night through.

records.source: Πρωΐας δὲ ἤδη γενομένης ἔστη Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλόν· οὐ μέντοι ᾔδεισαν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Early morning now already having come stood Jesus on the shore; not however knew the disciples that Jesus it is.

L.4: Now when early morning had already come, Jesus stood on the shore; the disciples, however, did not know that it was Jesus.

R.4: When morning came, Jesus was standing on the shore. But the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

decisions.choice: early morning: first light, at the end of the night
decisions.reason: The word means the early part of the morning, and "already" sets it just after the night of verse 3. It is the time when fishermen came in with their catch. John marked the same early hour when Mary came to the tomb (20:1).

decisions.choice: did not know that it was Jesus: the risen Jesus is not recognized until he makes himself known
alternatives: only because of the distance and the poor light
decisions.reason: The boat was about a hundred yards out (verse 8) and the light was dim, which may be enough to explain it. But Mary Magdalene also did not know him at first, close at hand (20:14), and the two on the road to Emmaus did not either (Luke 24:16). John does not give the reason; he tells how they came to know him.

decisions.choice: however: a sharp contrast; that it is: the present tense of their thought
decisions.reason: The word for "however" sets what the disciples did not know against the fact that Jesus was there. In reporting what they did not know, Greek keeps the tense of the thought itself: "that it is Jesus".

decisions.choice: Just as day was breaking (B); When morning came (R); realize (B)
alternatives: when early morning had already come (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the time in everyday words. Every level reports the thought "it is Jesus" in the past, "it was Jesus", as English does (meaning decision m3). Balanced says "realize" for "know", since the disciples could see the man but did not know who he was.

records.source: λέγει οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Παιδία, μή τι προσφάγιον ἔχετε;
records.gloss: Says therefore to them the Jesus: Children, not anything to-eat-with-bread do you have?

L.5: So Jesus says to them, "Children, you do not have anything to eat, do you?"

R.5: Jesus called out to them, "Friends, you do not have any fish, do you?"

decisions.choice: Children: a friendly, familiar way to call to a group of men
alternatives: little children, a teacher's tender address to his own disciples
decisions.reason: The word means "children", but it was also used in everyday speech to call out to young men or workmen, much like "lads". The disciples do not yet know who is speaking (verse 4), so to them it sounds like a friendly call from a stranger on the shore. When Jesus spoke tenderly to his disciples at the supper, John used a different word (13:33).

decisions.choice: anything to eat: something to eat with bread, usually fish
decisions.reason: The word means a relish or side dish eaten with bread, the main food of every meal. By the lake that was nearly always fish (compare 6:9, small fish with barley loaves). The question asks whether they have caught anything.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no"
decisions.reason: The Greek negative in the question shows that the speaker expects "no". He seems to know that they have nothing.

decisions.choice: Friends (B, R)
decisions.reason: Spoken to grown men, "children" sounds odd or belittling in English; "friends" gives the friendly tone of the address (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps the word.

decisions.choice: you do not have anything to eat, do you? (L); you have no fish to eat, have you? (B); you do not have any fish, do you? (R); called out (B, R)
decisions.reason: A question ending "do you?" or "have you?" shows that the answer "no" is expected (meaning decision m3). Balanced and Readable say "fish", which is what the word meant here (m2), and "called out", since he speaks from the shore to men in a boat.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ· Οὔ.
records.gloss: They answered him: No.

decisions.choice: No: a flat answer, as the question expected
decisions.reason: The one-word answer confirms what the question assumed: after a whole night they have nothing (verse 3).

decisions.choice: answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The disciples do not yet know that the man is Jesus (verse 4), but the pronoun refers to him, so it takes the reader setting for pronouns for God and Christ.

decisions.choice: No, we do not
decisions.reason: Readable completes the short answer, as English speakers would.

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Βάλετε εἰς τὰ δεξιὰ μέρη τοῦ πλοίου τὸ δίκτυον, καὶ εὑρήσετε.
records.gloss: He now said to them: Cast into the right parts of the boat the net, and you will find.

L.6: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find [some]."

R.6: He told them, "Throw your net out on the right side of the boat. Then you will catch some fish."

decisions.choice: the right side of the boat: simply the other side from where they had been fishing
alternatives: the side of favor or blessing
decisions.reason: In Scripture the right hand is often the side of honor (Psalm 110:1), and some readers have seen that here. The story gives no such hint: the point is that the catch comes when they do what Jesus says.

decisions.choice: you will find: a promise, with the object understood
decisions.reason: The verb has no object; from the question in verse 5 it is plain that fish are meant. The disciples obey a man they have not recognized, and the promise comes true at once.

decisions.choice: the net: a large fishing net let down from the boat
alternatives: a small cast net thrown by hand
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for a fishing net. This one was big enough to hold 153 large fish (verse 11) and too heavy for the crew to haul aboard (verse 6), so it was a large net worked from the boat.

decisions.choice: Throw ... out (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Cast" is the fisherman's word, but in everyday English "throw out" is plainer. Literal keeps "cast", because the same verb returns in the next sentence and in verse 7, where Peter "cast himself" into the sea.

decisions.choice: [some] (L); fish (B); catch some fish (R); your net (R)
decisions.reason: English needs an object for "find" (meaning decision m2). Readable says what they will find and uses the everyday "catch".

records.source: ἔβαλον οὖν, καὶ οὐκέτι αὐτὸ ἑλκύσαι ἴσχυον ἀπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἰχθύων.
records.gloss: They cast therefore, and no longer it to haul were they able from the multitude of the fish.

L.6: So they cast [it], and they were no longer able to haul it in because of the great number of fish.

R.6: So they did. Then there were so many fish in the net that they were not able to pull it in.

decisions.choice: haul: drag a heavy load, with a possible echo of Jesus drawing people to himself
alternatives: an ordinary word for hauling a net, with no echo
decisions.reason: The verb means to drag or pull something heavy; Peter uses it again in verse 11. John also uses it for the Father drawing people to Jesus (6:44) and for Jesus drawing all people to himself when he is lifted up (12:32). Some readers see the great catch as a picture of the people the disciples will bring in. John does not draw the link, and the word is the normal one for hauling a net.

decisions.choice: no longer able: now they could not, though the net had been light all night
decisions.reason: "No longer" sets the moment against the empty night before: suddenly the net is too heavy to haul. The tense pictures them trying and failing.

decisions.choice: because of the great number of fish
decisions.reason: The preposition gives the cause: the weight of so many fish.

decisions.choice: haul ... in (L, B); pull ... in (R)
decisions.reason: "Draw" is old-fashioned for a net. Literal and Balanced use "haul" here and in verse 11, so the repeated verb stays visible; Readable uses the plainer "pull" in both places.

decisions.choice: cast [it] (L); threw it out (B); So they did (R)
decisions.reason: The net is understood as the object; Literal brackets it. Readable says simply that they obeyed.

records.source: λέγει οὖν ὁ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος ὃν ἠγάπα ὁ Ἰησοῦς τῷ Πέτρῳ· Ὁ κύριός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Says therefore the disciple that whom loved the Jesus to the Peter: The Lord it is.

L.7: So that disciple whom Jesus loved says to Peter, "It is the Lord!"

R.7: The disciple whom Jesus loved told Peter, "It is the Lord!"

decisions.choice: the disciple whom Jesus loved: the unnamed disciple of 13:23, 19:26 and 20:2
decisions.reason: John never names him. He is one of the seven of verse 2, and 21:20-24 says that he is the disciple who wrote these things. As at the empty tomb (20:8), he is the first to see what has happened.

decisions.choice: So: the catch is what tells him who the stranger is
decisions.reason: The word "so" ties his recognition to the catch of verse 6: the great haul, after a night of nothing, at the word of the man on the shore, shows him that it is Jesus.

decisions.choice: the Lord: the risen Jesus
alternatives: the master, a title of respect only
decisions.reason: Since the resurrection the disciples speak of Jesus as "the Lord" (20:18, 20, 25), the title Thomas gave him in his confession (20:28).

decisions.choice: It is the Lord!
alternatives: The Lord it is (word for word)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the exact words, as a cry of recognition; the Greek puts "the Lord" first for emphasis, which the exclamation mark carries in English. "The disciple whom Jesus loved" stays the same at every level (see the book's terms).

records.source: Σίμων οὖν Πέτρος, ἀκούσας ὅτι ὁ κύριός ἐστιν, τὸν ἐπενδύτην διεζώσατο, ἦν γὰρ γυμνός, καὶ ἔβαλεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν·
records.gloss: Simon therefore Peter, having heard that the Lord it is, the outer garment tied around himself, he was for stripped, and cast himself into the sea;

L.7: So Simon Peter, having heard that it was the Lord, tied the outer garment around [himself], for he was stripped [for work], and cast himself into the sea.

R.7: When Simon Peter heard it was the Lord, he put on his outer coat and tied it, because he had taken it off to work. Then he jumped into the lake.

decisions.choice: stripped: lightly dressed for work, not necessarily naked
decisions.reason: The word means "naked", but it was also used of someone wearing only a short tunic or loincloth without an outer garment, as a man doing hard work might be. That is the natural picture for a fisherman at work in a boat. A footnote gives "naked".

decisions.choice: tied his outer garment around himself: put it on and belted it
alternatives: tucked up the clothing he was wearing
decisions.reason: The verb means to tie something around oneself; John used it of Jesus tying the towel around himself at the supper (13:4-5). It seems strange to put on more clothing before going into the water, but a Jew would not come before another person, least of all the Lord, without proper clothes, and a belted garment would not hinder him in the water. The exact action is not certain.

decisions.choice: threw himself into the sea: to reach Jesus ahead of the boat
decisions.reason: John does not say whether Peter swam or waded. The boat was about a hundred yards out (verse 8), and Peter does not wait for it. It is the same verb as "cast" the net in verse 6.

decisions.choice: stripped [for work] (L); had stripped for work (B); had taken it off to work (R)
decisions.reason: In English "naked" means wearing nothing, which is more than the Greek word need mean here (meaning decision m1). Literal brackets "for work", which the context supplies.

decisions.choice: his outer garment (B); put on his outer coat and tied it (R); threw himself (B); jumped (R); the lake (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday verbs. Readable spells out putting the coat on and tying it (meaning decision m2), and says "lake" for the sea, as it does in chapter 6.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι μαθηταὶ τῷ πλοιαρίῳ ἦλθον, οὐ γὰρ ἦσαν μακρὰν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀλλὰ ὡς ἀπὸ πηχῶν διακοσίων, σύροντες τὸ δίκτυον τῶν ἰχθύων.
records.gloss: The but other disciples in the little boat came, not for were they far from the land but about from cubits two hundred, dragging the net of the fish.

L.8: But the other disciples came in the little boat, for they were not far from the land, but about 200 cubits off, dragging the net of fish.

R.8: The other disciples came to shore in the boat, pulling the net full of fish behind them. They were not far from land, only about {{units:100 yards|200 cubits}}.

decisions.choice: the little boat: the same boat as in verse 3
alternatives: a small boat towed behind the fishing boat
decisions.reason: The word is a smaller form of the word for boat in verse 3, but John uses the two words for the same boats in 6:17-24. Nothing suggests a second boat.

decisions.choice: about two hundred cubits: about 300 feet, or 100 yards
decisions.reason: A cubit, the length of a forearm, was about 18 inches (45 cm), so two hundred cubits is about 300 feet (90 meters). The boat was near enough to shore for a man to swim or wade, and for the crew to tow in a net they could not lift.

decisions.choice: dragging the net: towing the net, full of fish, through the water
decisions.reason: They could not haul the net into the boat (verse 6), so they dragged it along in the water as they came in. Peter later hauls it ashore (verse 11).

decisions.choice: about {{units:100 yards|200 cubits}}
decisions.reason: A cubit means little to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give the distance in yards by default, and the units setting shows the original measure (meaning decision m2). Literal always keeps the ancient unit. Numerals are used in measurements.

decisions.choice: the boat (B, R); towing (B); full of fish (B, R); only (B, R); to shore, behind them (R)
alternatives: the little boat; the net of fish (Literal)
decisions.reason: "The net of fish" means the net full of fish. "Only" brings out the contrast of "not far ... but about". Balanced and Readable say "the boat", since it is the boat of verse 3 (meaning decision m1). Readable says where they were going and how the net came with them (m3).

records.source: Ὡς οὖν ἀπέβησαν εἰς τὴν γῆν βλέπουσιν ἀνθρακιὰν κειμένην καὶ ὀψάριον ἐπικείμενον καὶ ἄρτον.
records.gloss: When therefore they got out onto the land they see a charcoal fire lying and fish lying on [it] and bread.

L.9: So when they got out onto the land, they see a charcoal fire set there, and fish lying on [it], and bread.

R.9: When they got out of the boat on the shore, they saw a charcoal fire. There was fish cooking on it, and there was some bread.

decisions.choice: a charcoal fire: the same word as in 18:18, where Peter denied Jesus
alternatives: no connection between the two scenes
decisions.reason: This word for a fire of glowing charcoal is used only twice in the New Testament: in 18:18, where Peter stood warming himself at a charcoal fire and denied Jesus three times, and here, before Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him (21:15-17). John may mean the reader to remember the first fire at the second. The link rests on one word, so it cannot be proved.

decisions.choice: fish lying on it: fish cooking on the coals, the same word as for the fish in 6:9-11
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for the small fish eaten with bread at the feeding of the five thousand (6:9, 11). Jesus already has fish cooking before the disciples bring any of theirs. John does not say where it came from.

decisions.choice: fish ... bread: the Greek words are singular
decisions.reason: Both words are singular. They can mean a single fish and a single loaf, or fish and bread in general. John does not settle it, and verse 13 speaks of "the bread" and "the fish" in the same way.

decisions.choice: already there (B); cooking (R); saw (B, R)
alternatives: see a charcoal fire set there (Literal)
decisions.reason: The fire was laid and burning when they landed; Balanced brings this out with "already", and Readable says that the fish was cooking, which is what lying on the coals means. On "see" and "saw", see the historic present at verse 3. The words "fish" and "bread" can be singular or general in English, which keeps the question of meaning decision m3 open.

records.source: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐνέγκατε ἀπὸ τῶν ὀψαρίων ὧν ἐπιάσατε νῦν.
records.gloss: Says to them the Jesus: Bring from the fish which you caught now.

L.10: Jesus says to them, "Bring [some] of the fish which you have now caught."

R.10: Jesus told them, "Bring some of the fish you just caught."

decisions.choice: from the fish: some of them
decisions.reason: The preposition takes a part of the catch, not all of it.

decisions.choice: the fish you caught: their catch is added to the meal Jesus has made ready
decisions.reason: The word for fish is the same as in verse 9. Jesus already has fish on the fire, yet he asks for some of theirs, so that what they caught at his word is part of the meal. John does not explain the request.

decisions.choice: now: just now, this morning
decisions.reason: "Now" sets this catch against the empty night: these are the fish caught a moment ago at his word.

decisions.choice: [some] (L); some (B, R); have now caught (L); have just caught (B); just caught (R)
decisions.reason: English needs "some" to show the part taken (meaning decision m1); Literal brackets it. "Just" is the everyday English for "now" with a past action.

records.source: ἀνέβη οὖν Σίμων Πέτρος καὶ εἵλκυσεν τὸ δίκτυον εἰς τὴν γῆν μεστὸν ἰχθύων μεγάλων ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα τριῶν· καὶ τοσούτων ὄντων οὐκ ἐσχίσθη τὸ δίκτυον.
records.gloss: Went up therefore Simon Peter and hauled the net to the land, full of fish large, a hundred fifty three; and so many being not was torn the net.

L.11: So Simon Peter went up and hauled the net to the land, full of large fish, 153; and although there were so many, the net was not torn.

R.11: So Simon Peter climbed into the boat and pulled the net onto the shore. It was full of big fish, 153 of them. There were so many, but the net did not tear.

decisions.choice: went up: climbed aboard the boat, which had come to shore
alternatives: went up the beach to where the net lay
decisions.reason: The verb is used for getting into a boat (Mark 6:51; Matthew 14:32), and Peter needs to be at the boat to haul out the net that the others had dragged in. The Greek does not say "into the boat", so the sense "went up the beach" is also possible.

decisions.choice: a hundred and fifty-three: the count of a real catch
alternatives: a number with a hidden meaning
decisions.reason: Fishermen counted a catch in order to share it out or sell it, and an exact number fits the memory of someone who was there (21:24). Readers have also looked for a meaning in the number: for example, that it stands for the whole range of peoples to be gathered in by the disciples' mission. It is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 17, and the fishermen of Ezekiel 47:10 catch fish "of many kinds". John gives no hint that the number means more than the count.

decisions.choice: the net was not torn: so great a catch, and none lost
alternatives: a detail of the scene only
decisions.reason: The verb is the one the soldiers use of Jesus's seamless tunic, "Let us not tear it" (19:24), and the related noun is John's word for the divisions among people over Jesus (7:43; 9:16; 10:19). Some readers see the unbroken net as a picture of the one flock gathered by Jesus (10:16; 17:21). John says only that it held.
Numbers above ninety-nine are written in numerals at every level.

decisions.choice: went aboard (B); climbed into the boat (R); hauled (L, B); pulled (R); Even with so many, the net did not tear (B); There were so many, but (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where Peter went (meaning decision m1). "Hauled" and "pulled" repeat the verb of verse 6: what the crew could not do in the water, Peter now does on land. Readable makes the contrast its own sentence.

records.source: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Δεῦτε ἀριστήσατε.
records.gloss: Says to them the Jesus: Come, have breakfast.

L.12: Jesus says to them, "Come, have breakfast."

R.12: Jesus said to them, "Come and eat breakfast."

decisions.choice: have breakfast: eat the morning meal
decisions.reason: The verb means to eat the first meal of the day; it could also be used of a later meal, but here it is daybreak (verse 4) after a night on the water.

decisions.choice: Come: Jesus invites them as host
decisions.reason: The fire, the fish and the bread are his (verse 9), and he calls them to eat, as a host does. He then serves them himself (verse 13).

decisions.choice: eat your breakfast (B); eat breakfast (R); said (B, R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for the invitation. On "says" and "said", see the historic present at verse 3.

records.source: οὐδεὶς δὲ ἐτόλμα τῶν μαθητῶν ἐξετάσαι αὐτόν· Σὺ τίς εἶ;
records.gloss: None now dared of the disciples to question him: You who are?

L.12: But none of the disciples dared to question {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Who are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

R.12: None of the disciples were brave enough to ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Who are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

decisions.choice: none dared to ask: they felt awe before the risen Jesus
alternatives: they were simply too shy to ask a stranger
decisions.reason: They knew who he was (the next sentence), yet something in him made them want to ask and kept them from asking. The risen Jesus is the same Jesus, but not always known at once (20:14; Luke 24:16, 31), and the disciples stand in awe of him.

decisions.choice: question: ask closely, inquire
decisions.reason: The verb means to examine or inquire carefully (Matthew 2:8; 10:11). They did not dare to question him about who he was.

decisions.choice: You, who are you?: the pronoun is stressed
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "you" first, as in the questions put to John the Baptist (1:19) and to Jesus himself (8:25).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}; Who are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?
decisions.reason: The question would be spoken to Jesus, so "you" as well as "him" takes the reader setting for pronouns for God and Christ.

decisions.choice: Not one ... dared ask (B); None ... were brave enough to ask (R)
decisions.reason: "Ask" is the plain English verb for a question; "not one" keeps the force of "none". Readable uses everyday words for "dared".

records.source: εἰδότες ὅτι ὁ κύριός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: knowing that the Lord it is.

L.12: [They were] knowing that it was the Lord.

R.12: They knew that it was the Lord.

decisions.choice: knowing: the reason they did not ask
alternatives: knowing, and yet wanting to ask
decisions.reason: The participle belongs with "none of the disciples dared" in the sentence before; the SBLGNT puts a stop between them, but the sense runs on. They did not ask because they already knew the answer; the urge to ask shows how strange the meeting was (meaning decision m1 on the sentence before).

decisions.choice: the Lord: the risen Jesus, as in verse 7
decisions.reason: What the disciple whom Jesus loved said in verse 7, "It is the Lord", all of them now know.

decisions.choice: [They were] knowing (L); They knew (B, R)
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT makes these words a sentence of their own, so English needs a subject and a finite verb; Literal brackets what it supplies and keeps the participle.

records.source: ἔρχεται ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ λαμβάνει τὸν ἄρτον καὶ δίδωσιν αὐτοῖς, καὶ τὸ ὀψάριον ὁμοίως.
records.gloss: Comes Jesus and takes the bread and gives to them, and the fish likewise.

L.13: Jesus comes and takes the bread and gives [it] to them, and the fish likewise.

R.13: Jesus came over, took the bread, and gave it to them. He gave them the fish in the same way.

decisions.choice: takes the bread and gives it to them: an echo of the feeding by the same lake
alternatives: an ordinary host serving a meal, with no echo
decisions.reason: At the feeding of the five thousand, also by this lake, Jesus "took the loaves ... and distributed" them, "likewise also the fish" (6:11). Here he takes, gives, and does "likewise" with the fish. Readers may also think of the Lord's Supper, where Jesus took bread and gave it (Luke 22:19), though John does not mention a thanksgiving here. The words are also the plain way to describe a host serving a meal.

decisions.choice: the bread, the fish: the bread and fish already on the fire
decisions.reason: The article points back to the bread and fish of verse 9. Jesus serves them from what he has prepared.

decisions.choice: comes: Jesus comes over to them, by the fire
decisions.reason: John does not say where Jesus was standing; the verb shows him coming to where they were to serve them.

decisions.choice: came, took, gave (B, R); in the same way (B, R); came over (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the past tense (see the historic present at verse 3) and the everyday "in the same way" for "likewise". Readable makes the fish a sentence of its own.

records.source: τοῦτο ἤδη τρίτον ἐφανερώθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἐγερθεὶς ἐκ νεκρῶν.
records.gloss: This [was] already a third [time] was revealed the Jesus to the disciples having been raised out of dead.

L.14: This [was] now the third time Jesus was revealed to the disciples after being raised from [the] dead.

R.14: This was the third time Jesus showed {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} to the disciples after {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had been raised from the dead.

decisions.choice: the third time: the third appearance to the disciples as a group
alternatives: the third appearance of any kind
decisions.reason: John has told of two appearances to the disciples together: on the evening of the first day (20:19-23) and a week later with Thomas (20:26-29). This is the third. The appearance to Mary Magdalene alone (20:14-18) is not counted among appearances "to the disciples".

decisions.choice: was revealed: the same verb as in verse 1, closing the story
decisions.reason: Verse 1 opened with "Jesus revealed himself"; this verse closes with "Jesus was revealed". The passive keeps the sense of something made known, not just seen.

decisions.choice: after being raised from the dead: raised by God
alternatives: after rising from the dead by his own act
decisions.reason: The verb is passive, the usual way of saying that God raised Jesus (as in 2:22, "when he was raised from the dead"). John also records Jesus saying that he has authority to take his life up again (10:17-18); the two belong together.

decisions.choice: was revealed (B); showed himself (R); after he had been raised (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps "revealed" to match verse 1; Readable says "showed himself", as in verse 1. Balanced and Readable turn the participle into a clause with "he".

records.source: Ὅτε οὖν ἠρίστησαν λέγει τῷ Σίμωνι Πέτρῳ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Σίμων Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με πλέον τούτων;
records.gloss: When therefore they had eaten breakfast, says to the Simon Peter the Jesus, "Simon of John, do you love me more than these?"

L.15: So when they had eaten breakfast, Jesus says to Simon Peter, "Simon [son] of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} more than these?"

R.15: When they had finished eating, Jesus spoke to Simon Peter. "Simon, son of John," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} more than these others do?"

decisions.choice: love: the two verbs for love in 21:15-17 (ἀγαπάω, used by Jesus in his first two questions, and φιλέω, used by Peter in all three answers and by Jesus in the third question) are taken as having the same meaning here
alternatives: a distinction is meant: Jesus first asks for the fullest, self-giving love (ἀγαπάω), Peter can only answer with the love of a friend (φιλέω), and the third time Jesus comes down to Peter's own word
decisions.reason: John uses both verbs for the same love again and again: for the Father's love for the Son (3:35 ἀγαπᾷ; 5:20 φιλεῖ), for Jesus's love for Lazarus (11:5 ἠγάπα; 11:3 and 11:36 ἐφίλει), and for the disciple whom Jesus loved (13:23 ἠγάπα; 20:2 ἐφίλει). In this same passage he also varies the words for feeding and shepherding, for lambs and sheep, and for knowing (verses 15-17), with no change of sense. And verse 17 says Peter was grieved because Jesus asked a third time, not because he changed the verb. Still, the change of verb in the third question can be read as deliberate, and a footnote gives that view.

decisions.choice: more than these others love me
alternatives: more than you love these others
more than these things: the boat, the nets and the fishing (21:3)
decisions.reason: "These" can be masculine or neuter, and the comparison can be with what they do or with what Peter loves. Six other disciples are there (21:2), and Peter had once claimed a loyalty greater than theirs: he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37; compare Mark 14:29, where he says he will stand firm even if all the others fall away). The question would then ask whether that claim still stands after his denials. But the words can also ask whether Peter loves Jesus more than he loves his friends, or more than the fishing he has just gone back to (21:3). In his reply Peter does not compare himself with anyone.

decisions.choice: son of John (SBLGNT), as in 1:42 and in verses 16 and 17
alternatives: son of Jonah, or Jonas (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts read John here, as at 1:42; many later ones read Jonah, as in Matthew 16:17 ("Bar-Jonah"). This John is Peter's father, not John the Baptist. Jesus uses Peter's full name, the name he had when Jesus first met him (1:42), not the name Peter that Jesus gave him. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the meal by the charcoal fire recalls the night of Peter's denials
decisions.reason: Jesus has just given the disciples breakfast of bread and fish by a charcoal fire (21:9-13). The word for a charcoal fire (ἀνθρακιά) is used in the New Testament only here (21:9) and at 18:18, where Peter stood warming himself and denied Jesus. Jesus now asks him three times about his love, as Peter had three times said he was not a disciple (18:17, 25-27).

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R); also in verses 15, 16, 17 and 19
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("he says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in English. This applies to every "says" in the passage (verses 15, 16, 17 and 19). "Said" in verse 17 is already a past tense in Greek.

decisions.choice: love, for both verbs, at every level
alternatives: love (for the first verb) and be fond of, or love as a friend (for the second)
decisions.reason: Both verbs are "love" throughout John (meaning decision m1), so they are "love" here too, at Literal as well. To give them different English words would decide the question the footnote leaves open, and would make Peter's answer sound weaker than it need be.

decisions.choice: more than these others do (R); Jesus spoke to Simon Peter ... he said
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "more than these", which leaves the comparison open. Readable says what meaning decision m2 finds most likely, so it is marked uncertain.

records.heading: Jesus and Peter

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε.
records.gloss: He says to him, "Yes, Lord, you know that I love you."

L.15: He says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Yes, Lord; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

R.15: "Yes, Lord," Peter answered. "You know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: you know: Peter appeals to what Jesus himself knows
decisions.reason: "You" is stressed in Greek. After his denials Peter does not offer his own word as proof; he rests on Jesus's knowledge of him, which John has shown before (1:47-48; 2:24-25).

decisions.choice: Yes, I love you: Peter answers about his love but not about "more than these"
decisions.reason: Peter says yes to loving Jesus but makes no claim to love him more than the others. The man who once promised to lay down his life (13:37) now claims less. The verb he uses is the other verb for love (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: Lord: Peter's address to his risen master
decisions.reason: The disciples call Jesus "Lord" throughout John (6:68; 13:36-37), and in this chapter the disciple whom Jesus loved has just recognized him: "It is the Lord" (21:7).

decisions.choice: Peter said (B); Peter answered (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker so that the reader can follow who is speaking. Readable starts a new sentence at "You know", so that "You" takes a capital in any case.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ· Βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου.
records.gloss: He says to him, "Feed the lambs of me."

decisions.choice: the lambs are the people who belong to Jesus; Peter is given a shepherd's work
decisions.reason: Jesus has called himself the good shepherd and his followers his sheep (10:11-16). He calls them "my" lambs: they remain his, and Peter is to care for them on his behalf. In the Scriptures God holds the shepherds of his people to account for feeding the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-16; Jeremiah 23:1-4), and Peter later gives the same charge to the elders of the churches (1 Peter 5:2).

decisions.choice: lambs: young sheep, standing here for the flock as a whole
alternatives: only the young or weak believers, as distinct from the sheep of verses 16-17
decisions.reason: The word (ἀρνίον) is used only here in John's Gospel. It is a different word from "the Lamb of God" in 1:29. Jesus goes on to say "sheep" in verses 16 and 17 with no sign of a change of flock; the variation is most likely one of style (see the decision on verse 17).

decisions.choice: Jesus said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus as the speaker, since the last speaker was Peter.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ πάλιν δεύτερον· Σίμων Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με;
records.gloss: He says to him again a second [time], "Simon of John, do you love me?"

L.16: He says to him again, a second [time], "Simon [son] of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

R.16: For the second time Jesus asked him, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: the second question drops "more than these"
decisions.reason: Jesus no longer asks Peter to compare himself with the others; he asks only whether Peter loves him. He uses the same verb as in the first question (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: again, a second time: the question is repeated on purpose
decisions.reason: John counts the questions ("a second time", "the third time" in verse 17), so that the reader sees three questions answering Peter's three denials (18:17, 25-27).

decisions.choice: A second time he asked him (B); For the second time Jesus asked him (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek verb is the ordinary "says" in the present tense (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15); Balanced and Readable say "asked" because it introduces a question, and put "a second time" first, which also covers "again". Readable names Jesus.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε.
records.gloss: He says to him, "Yes, Lord, you know that I love you."

L.16: He says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Yes, Lord; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

R.16: "Yes, Lord," Peter answered. "You know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: Peter repeats his first answer word for word
decisions.reason: The answer is the same as in verse 15, with the same verb for love and the same appeal to what Jesus knows (meaning decisions m1 and m2 at 21:15, second sentence).

decisions.choice: the same English as Peter's first answer, at each level
decisions.reason: Each level repeats its wording of verse 15 exactly, so that readers hear the repetition the Greek has.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ποίμαινε τὰ πρόβατά μου.
records.gloss: He says to him, "Shepherd the sheep of me."

R.16: Jesus said to him, "Take care of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} sheep as a shepherd does."

decisions.choice: shepherd: do all of a shepherd's work, leading, guarding and providing for the flock
decisions.reason: The verb (ποιμαίνω) is wider than "feed" (βόσκω, verses 15 and 17): it covers the whole care of a shepherd for the flock. It shares a root with "shepherd" in 10:11-16, so Jesus gives Peter a share in his own work as the good shepherd. Peter uses the same verb when he charges the elders to shepherd God's flock (1 Peter 5:2).

decisions.choice: sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: little sheep: a diminutive form of the word (some early manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus)
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts read a diminutive form, "little sheep", here and in verse 17; others read the ordinary word for sheep, as the SBLGNT does. A diminutive like this was often used with no difference in meaning, so the sense is the same either way: the people who belong to Jesus (10:3-4, 14-16). A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Shepherd (L, B); Take care of ... as a shepherd does (R)
decisions.reason: "Shepherd" as a verb keeps the link with the good shepherd of 10:11-16 and keeps the two verbs of verses 15-17 apart (meaning decision m1). "Tend" is less common in everyday English. Readable spells out the picture in plain words.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ τὸ τρίτον· Σίμων Ἰωάννου, φιλεῖς με;
records.gloss: He says to him the third [time], "Simon of John, do you love me?"

L.17: He says to him the third [time], "Simon [son] of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

R.17: For the third time Jesus asked him, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: love: Jesus now uses the verb Peter has been using, with the same meaning as before
alternatives: Jesus lowers his question to the lesser love Peter has claimed
decisions.reason: Here Jesus takes up Peter's own verb (φιλέω). If the two verbs mean the same (meaning decision m1 at 21:15, which has the footnote), the question is simply asked a third time; if a distinction is meant, Jesus now meets Peter where he is. Either way, verse 17 gives the third asking itself as the reason for Peter's grief.

decisions.choice: the third time: the last of three questions
decisions.reason: With the article the phrase means "for the third time", completing the count begun in verse 16 ("a second time").

decisions.choice: A third time he asked him (B); For the third time Jesus asked him (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16: the present "says" becomes "asked" at Balanced and Readable because it introduces a question (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15). "Love" stays the same word as in verses 15 and 16 (rendering decision r-en-2 at 21:15).

records.source: ἐλυπήθη ὁ Πέτρος ὅτι εἶπεν αὐτῷ τὸ τρίτον· Φιλεῖς με;
records.gloss: Was grieved the Peter because he said to him the third [time], "Do you love me?"

L.17: Peter was grieved because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to him the third [time], "Do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

R.17: Peter felt very sad because Jesus asked him a third time, "Do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: Peter was grieved because he was asked a third time
decisions.reason: John gives the reason plainly: it was the third asking that hurt Peter. The verb (λυπέω) means to feel pain or sorrow, not to be offended.

decisions.choice: three questions recall Peter's three denials
decisions.reason: Peter had denied Jesus three times by a charcoal fire, as Jesus had foretold (13:38; 18:17, 25-27). Now, by another charcoal fire (21:9), Jesus asks him three times whether he loves him, and three times gives him the care of his flock. The third question would remind Peter of his third denial; it also lets him say three times what he had three times denied.

decisions.choice: the grief is at the third asking; whether the change of verb added to it is uncertain
alternatives: Peter was grieved because Jesus now used the other verb for love, as if doubting even the love Peter had claimed
decisions.reason: John repeats the question exactly as Jesus asked it the third time, with Peter's own verb. Those who see a distinction between the verbs take this as part of the hurt. But the sentence names "the third time" as the cause, not the choice of word (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: was hurt (B); felt very sad (R); Jesus asked (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Grieved" is formal in modern English. "Hurt" carries the pain of the Greek word without suggesting that Peter was offended; Readable uses the plainest words. Balanced and Readable name Jesus and say "asked", since "said" here introduces a question.

records.source: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Κύριε, πάντα σὺ οἶδας, σὺ γινώσκεις ὅτι φιλῶ σε.
records.gloss: And he said to him, "Lord, all things you know, you know that I love you."

L.17: And he said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, all things {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

R.17: Peter said, "Lord, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know everything. You know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: you know all things: Peter confesses what the disciples had said in 16:30
decisions.reason: On the night before the cross the disciples said, "Now we know that you know all things" (16:30). John has shown again and again that Jesus knows what is in people (1:47-48; 2:24-25; 6:64; 13:11). Peter now stakes everything on that knowledge, not on his own record.

decisions.choice: the two verbs for "know" (οἶδας and γινώσκεις) mean the same here
alternatives: you know all things in general; you recognize, by experience, that I love you
decisions.reason: Peter uses two different verbs for "know" in one breath. John uses both of Jesus's knowledge (2:24-25; 13:3, 7), and this passage varies its words throughout (see the decision on verse 17, last sentence). The second verb can be taken as knowledge gained by seeing and experiencing, but nothing in the sentence requires it.

decisions.choice: I love you: Peter's answer is the same in substance as before
decisions.reason: Peter uses the same verb for love as in his first two answers (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: know ... know, at every level
decisions.reason: The same English verb for both, because they mean the same here (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable drop the opening "And" and use normal English order; they name Peter, Balanced with "replied" since he is answering; Readable starts a new sentence at the second "You know".

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Βόσκε τὰ πρόβατά μου.
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "Feed the sheep of me.

decisions.choice: feed / shepherd and lambs / sheep: one charge in varied words
alternatives: three distinct tasks or three different groups (young believers, mature believers, and so on)
decisions.reason: Across verses 15-17 John varies almost every word: two verbs for love (verse 15), two for "know" (verse 17), "feed" (βόσκω) and "shepherd" (ποιμαίνω), "lambs" (ἀρνίον) and "sheep" (πρόβατον). Each pair is close in meaning, and the passage gives no sign that the variations mark separate groups or tasks. Together they give one charge: care for those who belong to Jesus, as he cares for them (10:11-16).

decisions.choice: sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: little sheep: a diminutive form (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16 (meaning decision m2 there), some manuscripts read the diminutive "little sheep"; the sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Jesus's words run on into verse 18
decisions.reason: The charge to feed the sheep leads straight into Jesus's word about how Peter will end his life (verses 18-19); the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11), and so will Peter.

decisions.choice: Feed, as in verse 15
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 15 gets the same English, so that "Feed" in verses 15 and 17 frames "Shepherd" in verse 16 as in the Greek. The quotation stays open because Jesus goes on speaking in verse 18.

records.source: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι, ὅτε ἦς νεώτερος, ἐζώννυες σεαυτὸν καὶ περιεπάτεις ὅπου ἤθελες· ὅταν δὲ γηράσῃς, ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σου, καὶ ἄλλος σε ζώσει καὶ οἴσει ὅπου οὐ θέλεις.
records.gloss: Amen, amen I say to you, when you were younger, you were girding yourself and were walking about where you were wanting; but when you grow old, you will stretch out the hands of you, and another you will gird and will carry where not you want.

L.18: Truly, truly I say to you, when you were younger, you used to put a belt on yourself and walk where you wanted; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will put a belt on you and carry [you] where you do not want [to go]."

R.18: I tell you the truth: when you were younger, you put on your own belt and went anywhere you wanted to go. But when you are an old man, you will stretch out your hands. Someone else will tie a belt around you and take you where you do not want to go."

decisions.choice: put on a belt: tie the long outer clothes up with a belt, ready to walk or work; done by another, it may also hint at being bound
alternatives: be tied up with ropes, as a prisoner
decisions.reason: People wore long, loose robes and fastened a belt round them before setting out or starting work (compare 13:4; Luke 12:35). A young man does this for himself and goes where he likes. When another does it for him, he is no longer free: the words fit a helpless old man being dressed, and they also fit a prisoner being bound and led away to die, which is how verse 19 explains them.

decisions.choice: stretch out your hands: most likely a veiled pointer to death by crucifixion
alternatives: the gesture of a helpless old man reaching out for someone to dress him and lead him
decisions.reason: Verse 19 says Jesus was showing by what kind of death Peter would glorify God, the phrase John used of Jesus's own crucifixion (12:33; 18:32). Greek and Roman writers sometimes spoke of the hands being stretched out of a person put on a cross, and Christian writers from about AD 200 onward say that Peter was crucified in Rome. Against this, the stretching out of the hands comes before the belt and the leading away, not after them. The words are a veiled saying, and the decision is marked uncertain.

decisions.choice: younger: when you were young, compared with now
decisions.reason: The word is the comparative of "young", contrasting Peter's earlier years with the old age to come (γηράσῃς, "you grow old"). It does not mean Peter is old now.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: put a belt on / fasten a belt / tie a belt (for the verb of girding); carry (L), take (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Gird" is no longer everyday English. Saying "belt" keeps the picture of the Greek, which allows both dressing and binding (meaning decision m1), rather than choosing one. The verb for "carry" is also used of leading or bringing someone; Balanced and Readable say "take". Literal supplies "you" and "to go", which the Greek leaves understood.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ εἶπεν σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ δοξάσει τὸν θεόν.
records.gloss: This now he said signifying by what kind of death he will glorify the God.

L.19: Now this {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God.

R.19: Jesus said this to show the kind of death by which Peter would bring glory to God.

decisions.choice: the narrator explains Jesus's words, with the phrase used of Jesus's own death
decisions.reason: John steps out of the scene to tell the reader what Jesus meant, in nearly the same words he used of Jesus's death ("signifying by what kind of death he was about to die", 12:33; 18:32). Peter will die as his Lord died. "Signifying" means pointing to something by a hint rather than saying it outright.

decisions.choice: Peter's death will glorify God
decisions.reason: In John the cross is where the Son glorifies the Father (12:23-28; 13:31-32; 17:1, 4). Peter's death, faithful to the end, will also bring glory to God.

decisions.choice: Peter (B, R); Jesus said ... bring glory to God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Peter, so that the second "he" is not taken as Jesus. Balanced keeps the wording of 12:33 ("He said this to show ..."). Readable names Jesus and says "bring glory to" for "glorify". It does not add "on a cross" as 12:33 does, because here the kind of death is less certain (meaning decision m2 at verse 18).

records.source: καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν λέγει αὐτῷ· Ἀκολούθει μοι.
records.gloss: And this having said, he says to him, "Follow me."

L.19: And having said this, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Follow me: the call to discipleship, now including following Jesus in death
decisions.reason: Jesus called his first disciples with these words (1:43). On the last night he told Peter, "You cannot follow me now ... but later you will follow" (13:36), and he had said that whoever serves him must follow him, and where he is, his servant will be (12:24-26). Now, after foretelling Peter's death, Jesus renews the call: Peter will follow him in life and, in the end, in the way he dies.

decisions.choice: Follow: keep on following
decisions.reason: The command is in the present tense, which in Greek points to a continuing way of life, not a single step.

decisions.choice: told him (B); Then Jesus said to Peter (R)
decisions.reason: The present "says" becomes a past tense (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15). Readable names both persons and puts "After saying this" as "Then". Every level keeps the short "Follow me" of 1:43 and 13:36.

records.source: Ἐπιστραφεὶς ὁ Πέτρος βλέπει τὸν μαθητὴν ὃν ἠγάπα ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀκολουθοῦντα, ὃς καὶ ἀνέπεσεν ἐν τῷ δείπνῳ ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος αὐτοῦ καὶ εἶπεν· Κύριε, τίς ἐστιν ὁ παραδιδούς σε;
records.gloss: Having turned, the Peter sees the disciple whom loved the Jesus following, who also reclined at the supper on the chest of him and said, Lord, who is the [one] handing over you?

L.20: Having turned around, Peter sees the disciple whom Jesus loved following, the one who also had leaned back on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} chest at the supper and said, "Lord, who is it that is handing {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} over?"

R.20: Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved. That disciple was following them too. At the last supper, this was the disciple who had leaned back against Jesus's chest and asked, "Lord, who is it that will betray {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

decisions.choice: the disciple whom Jesus loved: the unnamed disciple of 13:23, 19:26, 20:2 and 21:7
decisions.reason: The Gospel never names him. This sentence ties him to the night of the last supper, so that readers know which disciple is meant before verse 24 says that he is the one who testifies to these things and wrote them.

decisions.choice: who also had reclined ... and said: a reminder of 13:23-25, pointing back to that night
alternatives: a new event at a different meal
decisions.reason: "The supper" is the meal of 13:2, where this disciple lay next to Jesus and leaned back against his chest to ask who the betrayer was (13:25). The same verb and the same word for "chest" are used here. John recalls the scene to show who this disciple is: the one closest to Jesus on the night he was handed over.

decisions.choice: following: walking behind Jesus and Peter, with an echo of following as a disciple
alternatives: following only in the plain sense
decisions.reason: Jesus has just said to Peter, "Follow me" (verse 19), and the two seem to be walking together. The other disciple comes after them. John uses the same verb for following Jesus as a disciple (1:37-43; 8:12; 12:26), and verse 22 picks it up again, so the plain sense likely carries this second one as well.

decisions.choice: handing you over: betraying you, said of Judas
alternatives: handing over in a neutral sense
decisions.reason: As in 6:64, 6:71, 12:4 and 13:21, the verb means to hand someone over, and used of Judas it means betrayal. The present tense in the question at the supper spoke of what was about to happen.

decisions.choice: sees, says (L); saw, asked, said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he sees", "he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 20, 21 and 22).

decisions.choice: leaned back; Lord, who is it ...; handing you over (L); betray (B, R); following them (B, R); the last supper (R)
alternatives: Lord, who is the one betraying you?
decisions.reason: The recalled words keep the English of 13:25 ("leaning back", "Lord, who is it?"). As in 13:21, Literal keeps the plain sense of "hand over", and Balanced and Readable say what Judas's handing over was (meaning decision m4). Balanced and Readable supply "them" for the ones he followed, Jesus and Peter (m3), and Readable names the meal so that young readers know which supper is meant (m2).

records.heading: The disciple whom Jesus loved

records.source: τοῦτον οὖν ἰδὼν ὁ Πέτρος λέγει τῷ Ἰησοῦ· Κύριε, οὗτος δὲ τί;
records.gloss: This one therefore having seen, the Peter says to the Jesus, Lord, this one and what?

L.21: So, having seen this one, Peter says to Jesus, "Lord, and what about this one?"

R.21: When Peter saw him, he asked Jesus, "Lord, what will happen to him?"

decisions.choice: this one and what?: what will happen to him?
decisions.reason: The Greek is a short question with no verb. Jesus has just told Peter how he will die (verses 18-19), so the question most naturally asks about the other disciple's future: what will become of him? John does not say why Peter asked, whether from concern for his friend or from wanting to compare their lots.

decisions.choice: and: setting this disciple beside Peter himself
decisions.reason: The small word sets the other disciple against what has just been said about Peter: "and he?", "what about him, then?" Jesus's answer (verse 22) keeps the same contrast: "you, follow me".

decisions.choice: Lord: the address of a disciple to his master
decisions.reason: As at the supper (13:25, 36-37) and earlier in this chapter (21:15-17), Peter speaks to Jesus as "Lord".

decisions.choice: what about him (B); what will happen to him (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the short, open question; Readable says in full what it asks (meaning decision m1). Both use the past tense (see verse 20, rendering decision r-en-1).

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν ἕως ἔρχομαι, τί πρὸς σέ;
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, If him I want to remain until I come, what to you?

L.22: Jesus says to him, "If I want him to remain until I come, what [is that] to you?

R.22: Jesus said to him, "Suppose I want him to stay alive until I come back. What does that matter to you?

decisions.choice: remain: stay alive, go on living
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to live on, as in 12:34 ("the Christ remains forever") and 1 Corinthians 15:6, where most of the witnesses "remain" until now, that is, are still alive. That is the sense here: verse 23 shows that people took it to mean the disciple would not die. It is the same verb John uses for remaining in Jesus (15:4-10), but nothing in the context points to that sense here.

decisions.choice: if I want: a supposition, not a promise
alternatives: a promise that he will live until Jesus comes
decisions.reason: The form puts a case: "suppose that I want". Jesus does not say that he does want it, as verse 23 is careful to point out. What happens to the other disciple is Jesus's own choice, as Peter's death is (verses 18-19).

decisions.choice: until I come: Jesus's coming again at the end
alternatives: his coming to the disciples after the resurrection
his coming at a person's death
decisions.reason: Jesus has promised to come again and take his disciples to himself (14:3). The followers of verse 23 understood the words of his return, and the correction there does not dispute that sense; it only denies that Jesus made a promise. The present tense "I come" refers to the future, as often with this verb.

decisions.choice: what is that to you?: that is not your concern
decisions.reason: The phrase, literally "what to you?", tells Peter that the other disciple's future is not his business. Jesus turns him back from comparing to his own call.

decisions.choice: remain (L, B); stay alive (R); come back (R); what does that matter to you (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "remain", John's word throughout (see the book's terms), so that verses 22 and 23 read as the same saying that was misunderstood; the context makes the sense plain (meaning decision m1). Readable says "stay alive" and "come back" (m3), turns the "if" into "suppose" (m2) and puts the idiom into plain words (m4).

records.source: σύ μοι ἀκολούθει.
records.gloss: You me follow.

decisions.choice: you: stressed, in contrast with the other disciple
decisions.reason: The Greek does not need the pronoun with a command, so its presence, at the head of the sentence, puts weight on it: whatever happens to him, you are to follow me.

decisions.choice: follow me: go on following Jesus as his disciple, to the end
decisions.reason: The command repeats verse 19, and the present tense means to keep on following. After the words about Peter's death (verses 18-19) it also recalls 13:36, "you will follow me later": Peter is to follow Jesus even in dying for him. These are the last words of Jesus in the Gospel.

decisions.choice: As for you (B); But you must (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the bare "you"; Balanced and Readable show the stress and the contrast with the other disciple in natural words (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν οὗτος ὁ λόγος εἰς τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ὅτι ὁ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκει.
records.gloss: Went out therefore this the word to the brothers that the disciple that not dies.

L.23: So this word went out to the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, that that disciple does not die.

R.23: So word spread among the believers that this disciple would not die.

decisions.choice: the brothers: the community of believers, men and women
decisions.reason: On the day of the resurrection Jesus called his disciples "my brothers" (20:17). Here the word is used, as often in Acts and the letters (Acts 1:15-16; 9:30), for believers in general, the community that told and handed on the story. The masculine plural covers a mixed group.

decisions.choice: this word went out: the saying of verse 22 spread, understood in a certain way
decisions.reason: "This word" is Jesus's saying about the disciple remaining until he comes, or the conclusion people drew from it. It "went out", that is, it was passed on from person to person.

decisions.choice: does not die: the present tense, meaning that he would not die
decisions.reason: Greek keeps the tense of the words as they were first said. The believers took "remain until I come" to mean that this disciple would still be alive when Jesus returned.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} (L, B); the believers (R)
decisions.reason: The brothers are the whole community of believers, men and women (meaning decision m1), so the inclusive form is the default and "brothers" the alternative, as at 20:17. Readable says "the believers", which is already inclusive and needs no setting.

decisions.choice: spread; would not die
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the natural verb for news passing from person to person (meaning decision m2), and the tense that reported speech takes in this language (m3).

records.source: οὐκ εἶπεν δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκει ἀλλ’· Ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν ἕως ἔρχομαι, τί πρὸς σέ;
records.gloss: Not said however to him the Jesus that not he dies, but, If him I want to remain until I come, what to you?

L.23: But Jesus did not say to him that he does not die, but, "If I want him to remain until I come, what [is that] to you?"

R.23: But Jesus did not say that this disciple would not die. He only said, "Suppose I want him to stay alive until I come back. What does that matter to you?"

decisions.choice: what is that to you? is part of the quotation (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the quotation ends at "until I come"
decisions.reason: A few witnesses, among them the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some early translations, leave out the last words of the quotation. Most manuscripts repeat Jesus's words of verse 22 in full, and the SBLGNT prints them. The meaning is not affected. A footnote gives the shorter reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: not ... but: a correction quoting Jesus's exact words
decisions.reason: The writer sets the rumor against what Jesus actually said. By repeating the saying word for word, he shows that it was a supposition ("if I want"), not a promise, and leaves the disciple's future in Jesus's hands.

decisions.choice: the correction may suggest that the disciple had died, or was old, when this was written
alternatives: the correction was made while the disciple was still in good health, only to set the record straight
decisions.reason: If believers expected this disciple to live until Jesus returned, his death, or his great age, would have raised the question of whether Jesus had been wrong. The careful correction would meet that question. The text does not say so, and it is possible that the correction was made for another reason. Verse 24 speaks of the disciple's testimony in the present tense.

decisions.choice: Peter, the disciple (B); this disciple, only (R)
alternatives: to him that he does not die (L)
decisions.reason: In the Greek "him" is Peter and "he" is the other disciple; Balanced and Readable name each so that the pronouns are not confused. Readable gives "but" as "only", since the point is that Jesus said no more than this (meaning decision m2). The saying keeps the wording it has in verse 22 at each level.

records.source: Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ μαθητὴς ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ τούτων καὶ ὁ γράψας ταῦτα, καὶ οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀληθὴς αὐτοῦ ἡ μαρτυρία ἐστίν.
records.gloss: This is the disciple the [one] testifying concerning these things and the [one] having written these things, and we know that true of him the testimony is.

L.24: This is the disciple who testifies concerning these things and who wrote these things, and we know that his testimony is true.

R.24: This disciple is the one who tells about these things, and he is the one who wrote them down. We know that what he says can be trusted.

decisions.choice: this is the disciple: the disciple whom Jesus loved (verse 20)
decisions.reason: "This" points back to the disciple of verses 20-23. The Gospel ends by naming him as its witness, yet still does not give his name. He was at the supper (13:23), at the cross (19:26-27, 35) and at the empty tomb (20:2-8).

decisions.choice: wrote these things: wrote them himself, or had them written
alternatives: wrote down some of these things, later included in the book
decisions.reason: The verb normally means that he wrote. It can also be used of one who has something written, as Pilate "wrote" the title on the cross (19:19-22) though others will have done the lettering. The sentence may mean that the disciple wrote the Gospel with his own hand, or that he stands behind it as its source and author. "These things" may be the whole Gospel or the account just told; the next verse looks back over the whole book.

decisions.choice: we know: a group who vouch for the disciple's witness
alternatives: the writer speaking of himself as "we" (compare 1:14; 3:11)
decisions.reason: The sentence speaks of the disciple as "he" and then says "we know". The most natural reading is that others, perhaps the community that knew him and issued the Gospel, add their own word that his testimony can be relied on, as two witnesses make a testimony valid (8:17). The disciple himself could be speaking with others in the plural, as in 1:14 ("we have seen his glory"), or including his readers. John does not say who "we" are.

decisions.choice: testifying ... his testimony is true: an eyewitness whose account can be relied on
decisions.reason: "Testify" and "testimony" run through the Gospel (1:7, 34; 5:31-39; 8:13-18; 15:27). The words echo 19:35, where the one who saw testifies and "his testimony is true". The present "testifies" may mean that he is still bearing witness, in person or through the book.

decisions.choice: testifies, testimony (L, B); tells about, what he says (R); wrote (L); has written (B); wrote them down (R)
alternatives: caused these things to be written
decisions.reason: "Testify" and "testimony" are the words used elsewhere in John, and "his testimony is true" matches 19:35. Readable uses everyday words for the same ideas, as in 19:35. Every level keeps "wrote", which leaves the question in meaning decision m2 open, as the Greek does.

records.source: ἔστιν δὲ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ ἃ ἐποίησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ἅτινα ἐὰν γράφηται καθ’ ἕν, οὐδ’ αὐτὸν οἶμαι τὸν κόσμον χωρήσειν τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία.
records.gloss: There are now also other many things which did the Jesus, which if they should be written one by one, not even itself I suppose the world to contain the being written books.

L.25: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, which, if they were written one by one, I suppose not even the world itself would contain the books being written.

R.25: Jesus also did many other things. If every one of them were written down, I do not think the whole world would have room for all the books that would be written!

decisions.choice: the Gospel ends with "books" (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "Amen" at the end, as copyists often did at the close of a book; the earliest do not have it. It has been held that the first scribe of Codex Sinaiticus ended the Gospel at verse 24 and that verse 25 was added afterward, but photographs of the page taken under ultraviolet light show verse 25 written by the first scribe. Some manuscripts of one family place the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) after this verse. A footnote gives "Amen". A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: not even the world could hold the books: an overstatement for effect
decisions.reason: The writer does not mean a calculation. He says in a vivid way what 20:30 says plainly: what has been written is a small part of what Jesus did, and his works are beyond counting. "The world" here is the whole earth. Writers of the time used the same kind of figure to praise a subject too great to tell in full.

decisions.choice: I suppose: the only place in John where the narrator says "I"
decisions.reason: After the "we" of verse 24, a single writer speaks in the first person for the only time in the Gospel. It may be the disciple himself, or the one who finished the book; John does not say. The word is modest: it gives the writer's own judgment.

decisions.choice: many other things that Jesus did: all his deeds, not only the signs
decisions.reason: The sentence echoes 20:30 ("many other signs ... not written in this book") but widens it to everything Jesus did. With it the Gospel closes, as it opened (1:1-3), on the greatness of the one it is about.

decisions.choice: I suppose (L, B); I do not think (R); contain (L); hold (B); have room for (R); one by one (L); each one (B); every one of them (R)
decisions.reason: "Suppose" keeps the writer's modest tone (meaning decision m3); Readable says the same in everyday words, with an exclamation mark to show that the words are an overstatement (m2). Balanced puts "Jesus did many other things" first, as natural word order; Readable keeps the word "world", as every level does.
